latest_nl_proof:
Fix integers m >= 2 and g >= 0.

We must prove that the number N(m,g) of numerical semigroups of multiplicity m and genus g equals the cardinality of K_{m,g}, where K_{m,g} consists of all tuples x=(x_1,...,x_{m-1}) of positive integers such that
(1) x_1+...+x_{m-1}=g,
(2) for all i,j in {1,...,m-1}, if i+j<m then x_i+x_j >= x_{i+j}, and if i+j>m then x_i+x_j+1 >= x_{i+j-m}.

We will construct a bijection between:
A = {numerical semigroups S subseteq N0 with multiplicity m and genus g}
and K_{m,g}.

For convenience, for any integer r with 1 <= r <= m-1, write r mod m simply as the residue class r.

Step 1: From a numerical semigroup S of multiplicity m to a tuple x(S).

Let S be a numerical semigroup with multiplicity m. Since m is the least positive element of S, we have
0 in S,
m in S,
and 1,2,...,m-1 notin S.
In particular, in each nonzero residue class r modulo m, there is no element of S smaller than m+r.

For each r in {1,...,m-1}, consider the set
T_r = {n in S : n congruent to r mod m}.
Because N0 \ S is finite, all sufficiently large integers lie in S; hence each residue class modulo m contains some element of S, so T_r is nonempty. By well-ordering, T_r has a least element; denote it by w_r.
Since w_r congruent to r mod m, there is an integer x_r >= 0 such that
w_r = m x_r + r.
Because r notin S and w_r is the least element of S in residue class r, we cannot have x_r=0; thus x_r >= 1.
So we obtain a tuple
x(S) = (x_1,...,x_{m-1})
of positive integers.

We now show that x(S) satisfies the defining inequalities of K_{m,g}.

Take i,j in {1,...,m-1}.

Case 1: i+j < m.
Then w_i + w_j belongs to S by closure under addition, and
w_i+w_j = m(x_i+x_j) + (i+j).
This has residue i+j modulo m. Since w_{i+j} is the least element of S in that residue class, we have
w_{i+j} <= w_i+w_j.
Substituting w_{i+j} = m x_{i+j} + (i+j) gives
m x_{i+j} + (i+j) <= m(x_i+x_j) + (i+j),
so x_{i+j} <= x_i+x_j.
Hence x_i+x_j >= x_{i+j}.

Case 2: i+j > m.
Then
w_i+w_j = m(x_i+x_j) + (i+j)
= m(x_i+x_j+1) + (i+j-m).
Again this sum lies in S and has residue i+j-m modulo m, so by minimality of w_{i+j-m},
 w_{i+j-m} <= w_i+w_j.
Thus
m x_{i+j-m} + (i+j-m) <= m(x_i+x_j+1) + (i+j-m),
whence x_{i+j-m} <= x_i+x_j+1.
So x_i+x_j+1 >= x_{i+j-m}.

Therefore x(S) satisfies all the inequality conditions.

Next we compute its coordinate sum. For each residue class r in {1,...,m-1}, the numbers less than w_r and congruent to r mod m are exactly
r, m+r, 2m+r, ..., (x_r-1)m+r,
which are x_r numbers. None of them lies in S, by minimality of w_r. Conversely, every n notin S must have some residue r in {1,...,m-1} modulo m, because all multiples of m belong to S (since m in S and S is closed under addition), and then n must be one of those x_r numbers below w_r in residue class r; otherwise n >= w_r and n congruent r mod m, so n = w_r + qm for some q >= 0, and since w_r,m in S and S is closed under addition, we would have n in S, contradiction.

Hence the gaps N0 \ S are exactly the disjoint union, over r=1,...,m-1, of those x_r numbers in residue class r. Therefore
|N0 \ S| = x_1+...+x_{m-1}.
Since S has genus g, this equals g. Thus x(S) belongs to K_{m,g}.

So we have defined a map
Phi : A -> K_{m,g},
Phi(S)=x(S).

Step 2: From a tuple x in K_{m,g} to a numerical semigroup S(x).

Now let x=(x_1,...,x_{m-1}) be any element of K_{m,g}. Define
S(x) = {0} union {qm+r : r in {1,...,m-1}, q >= x_r} union {qm : q >= 1}.
Equivalently, S(x) consists of 0 together with all nonnegative integers n such that either n is a positive multiple of m, or if n congruent r mod m with 1 <= r <= m-1, then n >= m x_r + r.

We prove that S(x) is a numerical semigroup of multiplicity m and genus g.

First, 0 in S(x) by definition. Also all sufficiently large integers belong to S(x): indeed, if n=qm+r with 0<=r<=m-1 and q >= max{x_1,...,x_{m-1}}, then n is included. Therefore N0 \ S(x) is finite.

Second, m in S(x), and no positive integer less than m lies in S(x): for 1 <= r <= m-1, since x_r >= 1, the number r has quotient q=0 < x_r, so r notin S(x). Hence the least positive element of S(x) is m, so the multiplicity is m.

The main point is closure under addition. Let a,b in S(x). We must show a+b in S(x).

Write a = m q + i and b = m p + j with q,p >= 0, 0 <= i,j <= m-1.
We consider cases.

If i=0 and j=0, then a+b = m(q+p), a multiple of m, so a+b in S(x).

If i=0 and 1 <= j <= m-1, then because b in S(x), we have p >= x_j. Hence
a+b = m(q+p)+j
has quotient q+p >= p >= x_j, so a+b in S(x).
The case j=0 is symmetric.

It remains to treat 1 <= i,j <= m-1. Since a,b in S(x), we have q >= x_i and p >= x_j.

If i+j < m, then
a+b = m(q+p) + (i+j).
Because x satisfies the defining inequality, x_i+x_j >= x_{i+j}. Therefore
q+p >= x_i+x_j >= x_{i+j}.
So a+b belongs to S(x) in residue class i+j.

If i+j = m, then
a+b = m(q+p+1),
a positive multiple of m, hence a+b in S(x). No inequality condition is needed in this case.

If i+j > m, then
a+b = m(q+p+1) + (i+j-m).
Since x belongs to K_{m,g}, we have x_i+x_j+1 >= x_{i+j-m}. Thus
q+p+1 >= x_i+x_j+1 >= x_{i+j-m},
so a+b belongs to S(x) in residue class i+j-m.

Thus S(x) is closed under addition. Therefore S(x) is a numerical semigroup.

Now compute its genus. For each r in {1,...,m-1}, the integers congruent to r modulo m that are not in S(x) are exactly
r, m+r, ..., (x_r-1)m+r,
namely x_r integers. There are no missing multiples of m, because every multiple of m belongs to S(x). Hence
|N0 \ S(x)| = x_1+...+x_{m-1} = g,
using the defining condition of K_{m,g}. So S(x) has genus g and multiplicity m. Thus S(x) belongs to A.

This defines a map
Psi : K_{m,g} -> A,
Psi(x)=S(x).

Step 3: Phi and Psi are inverse maps.

Take S in A and let x=Phi(S). For each residue class r in {1,...,m-1}, by construction the least element of S in that class is w_r = m x_r + r. Since m is in S, every larger number in the same residue class, namely w_r + tm for t>=0, also lies in S; and no smaller number in that residue class lies in S. Also every positive multiple of m lies in S. Therefore S is exactly the set S(x) defined from x. Hence
Psi(Phi(S)) = S.

Conversely, take x in K_{m,g} and let S=Psi(x)=S(x). In residue class r, the least element of S is clearly m x_r + r, because numbers r,m+r,...,(x_r-1)m+r are excluded and m x_r + r is included. Therefore the tuple extracted from S by the construction of Phi is exactly x. Hence
Phi(Psi(x)) = x.

So Phi and Psi are inverse bijections between A and K_{m,g}. Therefore
N(m,g) = |A| = |K_{m,g}|.

This is exactly the desired statement.
role_in_parent: Translates the original theorem into a cardinality statement for the combinatorial sets K_{m,g}; this fixes the prior self-containment issue by inlining N0, numerical semigroup, multiplicity, and genus.
statement_nl: Let m be an integer with m >= 2 and let g be an integer with g >= 0. Define K_{m,g} to be the set of all tuples x = (x_1,...,x_{m-1}) of positive integers such that for all i,j in {1,...,m-1}, if i + j < m then x_i + x_j >= x_{i+j}, and if i + j > m then x_i + x_j + 1 >= x_{i+j-m}, and such that x_1 + ... + x_{m-1} = g. Let N(m,g) denote the number of numerical semigroups of multiplicity m and genus g, where N0 = {0,1,2,...}, a numerical semigroup means a subset S of N0 containing 0, closed under addition, with finite complement N0 \ S, the multiplicity means the least positive element of S, and the genus means the cardinality of N0 \ S. Then N(m,g) = |K_{m,g}|.

domain_restrictions: x_k are required to be positive integers for k ∈ {1,...,m-1}
Indices i,j are quantified over the finite set {1,...,m-1}
Conditional inequality case 1: only applies when i + j < m; then i + j ∈ {1,...,m-1}, so x_{i+j} is defined
Conditional inequality case 2: only applies when i + j > m; then i + j - m ∈ {1,...,m-1}, so x_{i+j-m} is defined
No explicit condition is stated for the remaining case i + j = m
Numerical semigroups S are subsets of ℕ0 containing 0, closed under addition, with finite complement in ℕ0
Multiplicity of S is the least positive element of S and is required to equal m
Genus of S is |ℕ0 \ S| and is required to equal g
statement_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every integer pair (m,g) with m ≥ 2 and g ≥ 0, the number N(m,g) of numerical semigroups S ⊆ ℕ0 with multiplicity m and genus g equals the cardinality of the set K_{m,g} of all tuples x=(x_1,...,x_{m-1}) of positive integers satisfying: (i) x_1+...+x_{m-1}=g and (ii) for all i,j ∈ {1,...,m-1}, if i+j<m then x_i+x_j ≥ x_{i+j}, and if i+j>m then x_i+x_j+1 ≥ x_{i+j-m}.
quantifier_order: For all m, g with m ≥ 2 and g ≥ 0
K_{m,g} = { x : (for all i,j in {1,...,m-1} subject to conditional cases, inequalities hold) AND (x_1 + ... + x_{m-1} = g) }
N(m,g) = #{ numerical semigroups S satisfying: multiplicity = m and genus = g }
Claim: for all such m,g, N(m,g) = |K_{m,g}|

witness_dependencies: Elements x ∈ K_{m,g} depend on parameters (m,g): x has length m-1 and must satisfy sum constraint x_1+...+x_{m-1}=g
The index-inequalities defining K_{m,g} depend on m through both the comparison thresholds (m) and index transforms (i+j and i+j-m)
